t.rio de janeiro carioca landscapes betwee:
Rio is the one big city where a motorbike ride can end in a rainforest. The coordinates here fall on the western flank of the Tijuca massif, the green mountain range that rises in the middle of the city and carries the Corcovado, the Pedra Bonita and the Pico da Tijuca. Floresta da Tijuca, now a national park, is one of the largest urban forests in the world, and it is also a replanted forest. In the nineteenth century the original Atlantic forest had been cut for coffee and charcoal, the city's springs were drying up, and the emperor's government started replanting the slopes. What you ride through today is a second-growth jungle that grew back from that effort.

The title of the ride, Carioca landscapes between mountain and sea, is a fair description. Within a few kilometres you can go from the beach at Barra or Copacabana to a cool forest road with monkeys in the trees, waterfalls in the creeks and a view that opens suddenly onto the lagoon, the sea and the granite domes. The roads inside the park climb and twist in tight bends, with a patchy surface, moss, fallen leaves and the occasional pothole, and the air is humid and smells of wet earth. Be careful in the rain, which comes fast.

Practical points matter in Rio. Fuel and food are easy to find in the city, and the neighbourhoods around Alto da Boa Vista and the Tijuca side have bakeries and small restaurants. Park carefully and keep valuables out of sight, and ask locals or your accommodation about which areas to avoid, as safety varies a lot between districts, especially after dark. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads, and motorcycles filter between lanes in a way that visitors take a day or two to understand.

Weather decides the day. Mist can cover the peaks and close down views, and summer afternoons bring heavy thunderstorms, so mornings are the best time for forest roads. The dry winter months, from May to September, are cooler and clearer. The park also has marmosets, coatis and many birds, and the sound of the forest, particularly at dawn, is surprisingly loud for a place so close to millions of people. A cold coconut water from a roadside stand is the correct reward.
t.valongo wharf archaeological site@-22.9,:
There is hardly any monument here, and that is part of what makes it powerful. The Valongo Wharf in Rio's port district is a sunken stone landing, unearthed in 2011 under the street when the area was being renovated, and it is believed to be the principal place where enslaved Africans arrived in the Americas. Historians estimate that hundreds of thousands of people came ashore at Valongo in the first half of the nineteenth century, after being shipped across the Atlantic in conditions that many did not survive. It was built in 1811 to move the trade away from the city centre, and was later covered by a new quay built for the arrival of a bride for the emperor. The stones lay hidden for the better part of two centuries.

UNESCO recognised the site in 2017 as a place of memory. The surrounding area, the Pequena África or Little Africa, was where freed people and their descendants built communities around the port, with samba, candomblé and street culture taking shape in this neighbourhood. Nearby sites like the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground for those who died soon after landing, add to the sense of how close the trade was to everyday life in the city.

For riders, this is an urban stop. The port district has been redeveloped as Porto Maravilha, with new tram lines, wide avenues and big museums, and the streets can be confusing with one-way systems and construction. Park only in a place you can see or that is attended, as street crime happens in parts of central Rio, and leave valuables behind. Weekday daytime is much busier than Sunday, when the district is quiet and easier to look around. Fuel is available in the city, though stations are fewer in the dense centre, so fill up on the outer roads.

Give it time. A guided walk through the district brings more than a quick photo, and the nearby Museum of Tomorrow and the Rio Art Museum are close enough to visit by the same afternoon. A cold drink and a pastel, the fried turnover sold everywhere, will do for a break. The Niterói side of Guanabara Bay is visible across the water, and the long bridge links the two cities. Be respectful: this is a memorial as much as an archaeological site.
t.serra da bocaina national park@-23.0,-44:
The Serra da Bocaina is the green wall that rises behind the coast between Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, the high end of the Serra do Mar, and the national park that covers it protects one of the largest surviving patches of Atlantic forest. Rain from the ocean falls on the slopes almost daily, and the result is a dense, dripping jungle of tree ferns, bromeliads, orchids and enormous trees, with waterfalls and rivers running down to the sea. Clouds sit on the ridge, and the air smells of wet leaves and earth.

This forest has a human history that is easy to miss. In the eighteenth century, gold from Minas Gerais was carried over this ridge on the Caminho do Ouro, the Gold Road, by mule train, to be shipped from the port at Paraty, and parts of the old stone-paved road still survive in the forest. The route was dangerous and heavily taxed, and pirates preyed on the ships. Paraty itself, a handsome colonial town about twenty kilometres away, is one of the best preserved in Brazil and is part of the UNESCO listing for Paraty and Ilha Grande, granted in 2019.

The riding is a pleasure. The highway between Paraty and Cunha climbs the escarpment in a long series of bends, passing waterfalls, viewpoints and thick forest, and the temperature drops noticeably as you gain height. Cunha, on the plateau on the other side, is a cool, quiet town known for its ceramics, fired in wood-burning kilns in a technique brought from Japan, and for cheese and mountain crafts. Fog can fill the road in the morning, and rain is frequent, particularly in summer, from December to March, so ride with care on wet tarmac and watch for slippery leaves. Winter days are drier and clearer.

Paraty, with about fifteen thousand people, has fuel, cafes, guesthouses and pousadas, and Cunha, about twenty-nine kilometres away, has services too, though there is none in between. Try a fish stew, or cachaça, the sugarcane spirit, which Paraty has long been known for. The park itself has hiking trails and requires entry fees at some points, so check opening times and trail conditions with local guides.
Congonhas is a town of steelworks and iron ore in the hills of Minas Gerais, and on its highest ridge stands one of the great works of Brazilian art. The Sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Matosinhos is a pilgrimage church that looks out across the valley, and in front of it, along a stepped terrace, stand twelve Old Testament prophets carved from soapstone by the sculptor Antônio Francisco Lisboa, known as Aleijadinho, the Little Cripple. Their gestures are dramatic and slightly twisted, their faces intense, and they seem to speak across the town below.

The story of the sanctuary is tied to the gold rush. A Portuguese miner, Feliciano Mendes, is said to have vowed to build a church after recovering from illness, and the sanctuary was built from the 1770s with money from the mines. The prophets were carved in the early 1800s. Below the terrace, along the hillside path, six small chapels, the Passos, hold life-size wooden figures of the Passion of Christ, also attributed to Aleijadinho and his workshop. Aleijadinho was probably the son of a Portuguese builder and an enslaved African woman, and he worked despite a disease that deformed his hands, using tools tied to them, according to tradition. UNESCO inscribed the sanctuary in 1985.

For riders, the approach is along the BR-040, the busy highway between Belo Horizonte and Rio, or through smaller roads across the Serra de Ouro Branco, with views of rolling hills, mines and eucalyptus plantations. Traffic includes heavy lorries, and the weather can be wet from November to March. The town centre is steep, and the sanctuary's cobbled forecourt can be slippery after rain. Mornings are quiet, while weekends bring pilgrims and school groups.

Congonhas has fuel stations, restaurants and hotels, and Ouro Branco, a larger neighbour seventeen kilometres away, has more. Try pão de queijo, warm cheese bread, and tutu de feijão, a bean dish with pork, which are staples of Minas cooking. Leave plenty of time to walk the terrace slowly and look at each prophet in turn.
t.historic town of ouro preto@-20.4,-43.5:
Ouro Preto means Black Gold, and the name comes from the dark, iron-stained metal that miners found in the streams around here in the 1690s. The strike set off one of the biggest gold rushes in history, and within a few decades the town, then called Vila Rica, had become the richest in Brazil and one of the largest in the Americas. Today the gold is gone, but the town is still a spectacular set of whitewashed houses, baroque churches and steep, cobbled streets draped over a series of hills.

The wealth built dozens of churches, many decorated with gold leaf, and it also built a community of artists and writers who began to think of themselves as something other than colonial subjects. In 1789 a group of intellectuals in Vila Rica plotted a rebellion against the Portuguese crown, and the plot was betrayed. Its best known figure, an army officer nicknamed Tiradentes, was executed in 1792 and became a national hero. The sculptor Aleijadinho worked here, and his church of São Francisco de Assis is regarded as a masterpiece of Brazilian baroque. UNESCO made the town the first Brazilian World Heritage Site in 1980.

The riding is more of a challenge than it looks. The roads into town, from Belo Horizonte or from Mariana nearby, wind through the hills, passing old mining villages, and inside the centre the streets are steep and paved with rough stones, polished smooth and very slippery when wet. Parking and manoeuvring a heavy bike here takes patience. Rain is frequent from November to March, and mornings in winter can be misty and cool. Evenings, when the lanterns come on and the church bells ring, are magical.

Ouro Preto has fuel stations at the edge of town, plenty of pousadas in old houses, and restaurants serving the hearty food of Minas Gerais, such as tutu, pork and collard greens. Mariana, about nine kilometres away, is a smaller colonial town with its own churches and is easy to combine. Leave the bike at your accommodation and explore on foot. The student population gives the town a lively evening scene.
t.tijuca forest@-22.9,-43.3:
Tijuca Forest sits in the middle of Rio de Janeiro, a mass of green hills that rises right out of the dense city and holds the Christ the Redeemer statue on its peak. It is one of the largest urban forests in the world, and the astonishing thing is that it is not original. In the nineteenth century, coffee plantations and logging stripped these slopes, and the springs that supplied the city began to dry up. In 1861, Emperor Pedro II ordered the land to be replanted, and a major named Manuel Gomes Archer led a team of enslaved labourers who planted tens of thousands of saplings, an early and successful experiment in forest restoration.

Today the forest is a tangle of Atlantic rainforest, with waterfalls, hiking trails, viewpoints and small chapels. Toucans, marmosets, coatis and many butterflies live here, and you may hear them before seeing them. The Christ the Redeemer statue, finished in 1931, stands on Corcovado, one of the forest's peaks, about 30 metres tall on top of an 8 metre base, and it can be reached by a cog railway or through the forest roads.

The roads here are a great diversion for riders who like twisting climbs. Narrow, shady lanes wind up through the trees, with sharp bends, old stone walls and occasional hairpins, and some surfaces are cobbled or patched. Mist and sudden rain are common, and slippery leaves lie on the tarmac. Weekends bring cyclists and families, so go on a weekday morning. The temperature in the forest is a few degrees cooler than in the city. Stick to main roads and busy areas, and be aware that, as in any big city, petty crime does occur at some quiet viewpoints, so do not leave the bike unattended with valuables.

Rio de Janeiro has fuel stations throughout, workshops and every kind of lodging. Several cafes sit at the entrances of the park. Try a fresh coconut water from a kiosk and a plate of feijoada, the black bean and pork stew traditionally served on Saturdays. Bring a rain jacket, because the forest creates its own weather.
t.almaty@43.2,76.9:
Almaty means place of apples, or near enough, and the apples are not just a name. Wild apple forests, the ancestors of many of the world's cultivated varieties, still grow on the slopes of the Tian Shan mountains above the city, and botanists believe the fruit began its long journey to the world's orchards somewhere in this region. For most of the twentieth century Almaty was the capital of Kazakhstan, until the government moved to Astana in 1997, and it remains the country's biggest and most relaxed city, with wide tree-lined avenues, Soviet blocks and a skyline of snow peaks to the south.

The mountains are the heart of the place. The Trans-Ili Alatau range rises directly behind the city, and within half an hour you can be at the Medeu skating rink, high in a valley at about 1,700 metres, and from there ride a cable car up to Shymbulak ski resort. In the city, the Zenkov Cathedral, a wooden Orthodox church built in 1907 without a single nail, survived the great earthquake of 1911 that destroyed many stone buildings, and it stands in Panfilov Park as a quiet landmark. The Green Bazaar sells dried fruit, horse meat sausage, honey and fermented mare's milk.

For riders, Almaty is the starting point for the eastern run toward Charyn Canyon and the Kolsai lakes. The road east leaves the city through suburbs and then crosses open steppe, with the snowy Tian Shan on the right and wide flat country on the left, and it is fast and straight in places, with rough sections and sudden potholes. The canyon, about two hundred kilometres from the city, is a gorge of red sandstone sculpted into towers and walls, often called the Valley of Castles. The Kolsai lakes lie in a green valley higher in the mountains, reached by a winding road that is rough in spots and often wet. Weather in the high country changes quickly, with cold rain and even snow in summer.

Fuel stations and workshops are plentiful in the city and along the main road, though stations thin out in the mountains. Foreign riders should check entry rules, documents and insurance in advance. Traffic in the city is heavy, with aggressive driving, and the mornings and evenings are slow. Spring and early autumn are the best times for the ride, and the evenings in the city, with outdoor cafés full of people, are warm and lively.
t.mariana@-20.4,-43.4:
Mariana is where Minas Gerais begins, at least on paper. It was the first town the Portuguese founded in the gold country, in 1696, and later the first capital and first bishopric of the whole captaincy. It was named for Maria Anna of Austria, the queen of João V, which tells you who the town was meant to impress. Today it sits at around seven hundred metres in a bowl of green, forested hills, a calm university and mining town of some forty-five thousand people, and it is the natural place to begin the Estrada Real, the old colonial road along which gold and diamonds went to the coast and everything else came back up.

Park somewhere near the central square, Praça Minas Gerais, and walk. The pillory stands in the middle, where punishments were once carried out in public, and two baroque churches face each other across the square like a pair of well-dressed neighbours who have not spoken in a century. The cathedral has a German baroque organ that is still played, and on some days there are recitals. The streets are narrow, steep and cobbled in the old centre, so leave the bike on the edge and wear boots you can walk in.

Be aware that the mining that built Mariana is still its economy. Iron ore trucks share the road, and the 2015 collapse of the Fundão tailings dam, which buried the village of Bento Rodrigues a few kilometres away, is not something locals treat as history. It is worth being quiet and respectful about it if the subject comes up.

For the ride itself, the road to Ouro Preto is a short, pleasant one of nine kilometres or so, with rolling curves through hills the colour of rust and moss. It is also the route of a tourist steam train that runs on weekends, so you may find yourself racing a locomotive. Traffic is heavier in the afternoon and on weekends, and potholes appear without warning, particularly after rain, so keep your speed honest. Fuel, cash machines and plenty of food are all in town; the local places serve the Minas staples of beans, pork, cassava and kale, and a small coffee afterwards is almost obligatory. The dry months from May to September are the best time, with clear skies and cool mornings, while the wet summer brings afternoon downpours that turn those cobbles into glass.
t.ouro preto@-20.4,-43.5:
Ouro Preto means black gold, after the dark, iron-stained nuggets that set off the rush here at the end of the seventeenth century. For a while this town, then called Vila Rica, was among the richest and most populous places in the Americas, and its money went into churches, bridges, fountains and the steep, tilted streets you will be climbing and descending. UNESCO listed it in 1980, among the very first Brazilian sites, and walking in the centre you can see why: hardly a modern building disturbs the skyline of terracotta roofs and whitewashed towers climbing the hillsides.

The famous name here is Aleijadinho, the sculptor and architect Antônio Francisco Lisboa, who is said to have worked on after a disease deformed his hands, strapping tools to his wrists. His church of São Francisco de Assis is the one to see, and his carved soapstone saints run through the whole district. Soapstone is also what you will see sold in every other shop, in the form of cups, pots and little figures. The town's political history is just as rich. In 1789 a circle of local intellectuals and officials, the Inconfidência Mineira, plotted a revolt against Portuguese taxation, and one of them, the dentist known as Tiradentes, was hanged for it in Rio. Brazil celebrates him as a national hero every April.

On a motorcycle, Ouro Preto is a place to treat with a bit of humility. The streets are paved with irregular stones, often steep, polished by centuries of wheels, and wet in the rainy season, so a loaded touring bike can be a handful. Many riders park at the edge and explore on foot or take a short taxi, which is not a bad idea. Altitude is a little over a thousand metres, which keeps evenings cool, even a bit chilly in winter.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a town of sixty-odd thousand, and the university and its students give it a lively evening life that most heritage towns lack. Try the Minas cooking in a family restaurant, with beans, pork and greens, and finish with a goiabada and white cheese pudding. Mariana is nine kilometres away, so the two towns are easily done together, but give Ouro Preto the longer stay if you can, ideally with a night under a tiled roof.
t.carioca mountaion range tijuca national@:
Rio de Janeiro is a city that was clearly arranged by a geologist with a sense of humour. Granite domes rise straight out of the sea and the streets, and the Carioca mountains run through the middle of the city, so that the natural forest is a few minutes from the beaches. UNESCO's listing, called the Carioca Landscapes between the Mountain and the Sea, includes Tijuca National Park, the Botanical Garden, Sugarloaf, Copacabana and Corcovado, the peak where the statue of Christ the Redeemer opens his arms over the city. The statue is thirty metres tall, stands on an eight-metre base at about seven hundred metres above the sea, and was inaugurated in 1931.

Tijuca Forest has a surprising history. In the nineteenth century, the hills were cleared for coffee plantations, the streams dried up, and the city began to run short of water. The emperor ordered the land bought back and replanted, and a major named Archer and a small team of workers planted tens of thousands of saplings over thirteen years. The result is one of the largest urban forests in the world, home to marmosets, coatis, toucans and hundreds of butterfly species. The tall trees now standing on those slopes were planted by hand.

For a rider, the roads of Tijuca are among the best in the city, though they are not long. Narrow, twisting lanes climb through the trees, with hairpins, cobbled sections and old stone walls, passing viewpoints such as the Vista Chinesa and the Mesa do Imperador. Road conditions are variable, with tree roots, potholes and slippery leaves, and rain is frequent. Parts of the park roads are closed at times, so check the situation before you go. Traffic in the city below is fast and chaotic, with buses and motorbike couriers weaving between lanes, and security needs thought. Ask locals which areas to avoid, do not leave the bike unattended, and keep valuables out of sight.

Fuel is plentiful in the city, although stations in the tourist areas can be pricey. The best months are from May to September, when the humidity falls and the views are clearer. Summer brings heat, thunderstorms and crowds. Early morning is the best time for both the ride and the views, before the clouds gather on the peaks and hide the statue. Finish with fresh coconut water from a stand on the beach, which is the correct reward.
t.tiradentes@-21.1,-44.2:
Tiradentes is a small colonial town in the hills of Minas Gerais, in south-eastern Brazil, where the paving is cobbled stone, the church is full of gold, and the streets run uphill toward the Serra de Sao Jose. It has about four and a half thousand people and a calendar crowded with festivals, and the bigger town next door, Sao Joao del Rei, with nearly eighty thousand, is where you find supermarkets and a wider choice of fuel stations.

The history starts with gold. In the eighteenth century prospectors poured into this region, and the Estrada Real, the Royal Road, was the route the Portuguese crown used to haul the metal to the ports of Paraty and Rio de Janeiro under tight control. The town was founded as Sao Jose del Rei and renamed after Joaquim Jose da Silva Xavier, nicknamed Tiradentes, the dentist who joined the Inconfidencia Mineira, a plot against Portuguese rule in 1789, and was hanged in Rio in 1792. He is a national hero, and Brazil marks the anniversary of his execution as a public holiday on the twenty-first of April. The Matriz de Santo Antonio, the main church, is a baroque jewel with an interior gilded in great quantity.

Riding in is slow by design. The roads around climb gently through green hills of coffee, cattle and eucalyptus, with short sections of broken asphalt and occasional potholes after the rains, and local drivers pass in surprising places. Cobbles in town are slippery after rain and rough on a loaded bike, so take it gently and park where the locals do. A steam train called the Maria Fumaca still runs the short route to Sao Joao del Rei on selected days, a nice thing to see even if you do not take it.

Food is the Mineira kind: feijao tropeiro with beans, sausage and cassava flour, pao de queijo, slow-cooked pork, and strong coffee, with cachaca from the region's distilleries. Cooler mornings in the dry season, around May to September, are the best time, while the rainy summer brings storms in the afternoon.
t.bokonbaevo@42.1,77.0:
Bokonbaevo is a village on the south shore of Issyk-Kul, the great mountain lake of Kyrgyzstan, which lies at about 1,600 metres and is the second-largest alpine lake in the world. The name means warm lake, because the water, though cold, never freezes, even in the hard winters of the Tian Shan, and the mountains that rise behind it, the Terskey Ala-Too, carry snow all summer. On the road along the shore the lake is a sheet of deep blue on one side and the red and grey peaks on the other, and the contrast is striking.

The village is known for its eagle hunters, called berkutchi, who train golden eagles to hunt foxes and hares, a tradition that goes back centuries among the Kyrgyz and Kazakh peoples. Visitors can watch demonstrations, and a festival in winter and a small hunting display in summer keep the practice alive. The eagles are impressive birds, with wingspans of over two metres, and watching one fly from a hunter's arm across the open steppe is unforgettable. A few kilometres away, the little town of Kadzhi-Say, once a coal-mining settlement from the Soviet era, has a bleak, post-industrial feel, but nearby the red sandstone canyon known as Skazka, the Fairy Tale, has weird, eroded cliffs and rocks.

The riding along the south shore is a pleasure. The road is paved but rough in patches, with potholes, frost heave and occasional animals, and traffic is light apart from minibuses and trucks. Sudden winds off the lake can be strong, and the weather changes rapidly, so carry warm and waterproof clothing even in summer. Side roads head up into valleys with yurt camps, waterfalls and glaciers, mostly unpaved, and require care and decent tyres.

Fuel is available at stations along the shore, but not everywhere, so keep the tank topped up and carry a little extra if heading into the valleys. Food is simple and good: lagman noodles, beshbarmak, a dish of boiled meat and noodles, fresh bread, and fermented mare's milk, called kumis, offered in summer at roadside stalls and yurts. Apricots and berries are sold along the road in season.

Plan to stay a night in a homestay or a yurt camp, and wake early to see the sun come up over the lake. The silence and the clear air at this altitude are the real reward.
t.city of balasagun@42.7,75.3:
A single brick tower stands alone on the steppe south of the Chu river, and that tower is nearly all that remains of Balasagun, a city that once rivalled the great towns of the Silk Road. It was a capital of the Karakhanids, a Turkic dynasty that ruled much of Central Asia around the tenth to twelfth centuries, and it was here that the poet Yusuf Balasaguni wrote the Kutadgu Bilig, an early work of Turkic literature on how to govern and live well. Today the site is known as Burana, and Tokmok, eleven kilometres away, is the town you pass on the way.

The tower was once a minaret of perhaps forty-five metres. An earthquake brought down the top in the fifteenth century or thereabouts, and it now stands at about twenty-five, with a spiral stair inside that you can climb in the dark, hand on the wall. Around it lie the grassy outlines of a mausoleum, the foundations of the old citadel, and a row of weathered carved stones called balbals, set up on the steppe by earlier nomads to mark graves, each a rough human figure with hands folded at the belly. Wind plays across the grass.

The ride here comes from Bishkek, about sixty kilometres to the west, along a good road through the Chu valley, flat farmland of maize, sunflowers and poplar windbreaks, with the snow line of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too range standing to the south like a painted wall. The valley is wide and the traffic is mixed, with minibuses, lorries and the occasional horseman, so keep an eye on the verges. Summer afternoons are hot, but mornings are clear and the mountains are sharp. Spring is lovely, with fruit blossom and green slopes.

Tokmok is a real town with fuel, cafes and shops, so fill up and eat there; a plate of lagman noodles or fresh flatbread and a pot of tea will do nicely. The site has a small museum and an entry fee, and the old mound is open to wander. Ask a local if the stair is open, and watch your head. It is an easy, quiet stop that gives a sense of how far this region's history goes back.
t.saty@43.1,78.4:
Saty is a village at the end of a good road, and it looks it. The pin lies a little south of the settlement, in the northern Tien Shan, in Kazakhstan's far south-east, where the Kungey Alatau range rises in snow-streaked ridges along the border with Kyrgyzstan. Here the steppe gives way to green pastures dotted with spruce, and in summer, herders bring their horses and sheep up from the valleys and live in yurts on the hillsides. The air is clean and cold, the skies are huge, and the few buildings look small beside the mountains.

The great draw is the Kolsai lakes, a chain of three alpine lakes in a high valley a little farther on, each higher and colder than the last, the lowest at around eighteen hundred metres. A rougher track continues to nearby Kaindy, a lake that was formed by an earthquake in 1911 which caused a landslide to dam a gorge, leaving the trunks of drowned spruce standing in the clear turquoise water like ghostly masts. Both are popular with hikers and horse riders, and the region is also known for its fine wild apples, a reminder that the name of Almaty, the former capital, comes from the Kazakh word for apple.

Riding in this region is serious adventure. The road to Saty is paved for much of the way from Kegen, but surfaces vary, with potholes, loose gravel and occasional animals on the road, particularly cows, horses and sheep. Because the area is near the Kyrgyz border, there are checkpoints, and you may need a border-zone permit to visit the lakes, so check the rules before you go. Weather can change in minutes, with cold rain and even snow in summer, and the dirt tracks can be very muddy.

Fuel is not available in Saty itself, so fill in Kegen or in Almaty, and carry extra if you can. Simple guesthouses offer meals of lamb, bread and tea, and in summer you may be offered kumys, fermented mare's milk, which is an acquired taste. The best months are June to September. Bring warm layers, even in July, and plenty of cash in local currency, since cards are rarely accepted outside the larger towns.
t.jeti oguz@42.3,78.2:
Jeti Oguz means seven bulls, and the name belongs to a line of rust-red sandstone cliffs that rise above a pine-dotted valley on the southern side of Lake Issyk-Kul, in the Tien Shan mountains of eastern Kyrgyzstan. The cliffs are jagged and stacked side by side, and local legend says they are the petrified remains of seven bulls. A second formation, a red rock split down the middle in the shape of a heart, is known as the Broken Heart, and it is surrounded by a story of two rival suitors and a murdered khan that every guide tells slightly differently.

The valley sits at around 2,200 metres, and the air is clear and cool, scented with spruce and mountain grass. Soviet-era sanatoriums, which used the mineral springs and clean air to treat holidaymakers, still stand beside the river, some in use and some falling into ruin, giving the valley a faintly melancholy air. In summer, shepherds' families set up yurts on the high pastures, called jailoo, and herds of horses, sheep and cattle graze across the slopes. You can often buy kymyz, fermented mare's milk, or fresh bread and honey at a yurt, and the hospitality is generous.

The road to the valley leaves the lake shore near Kyzyl-Suu and follows a stream upward, paved at first and then increasingly rough, with loose stones, potholes and fords. It is not a difficult ride in summer, but in wet weather or after snow it can be demanding, and you should be prepared for river crossings in early summer when snowmelt is high. The mountains above hold snow well into July.

Karakol, about twenty-two kilometres away, is the nearest large town, with fuel stations, shops and guesthouses, and Kyzyl-Suu, closer, is smaller but has basic services.

Finishing here, among red cliffs, spruce and grazing horses, is a satisfying end to the ride around the lake. Take time to walk among the trees, and try a bowl of hot lagman noodles from a roadside cafe before heading back.
t.karakol@42.5,78.4:
Karakol is the largest town on the eastern end of Lake Issyk-Kul, a place of about seventy thousand people at the foot of the Terskey Ala-Too range, and it is full of surprises. It was founded as a Russian garrison in the 1860s, and it has kept a good deal of its nineteenth-century character, with low wooden houses, painted shutters and tree-lined streets. The Holy Trinity Cathedral, a wooden Orthodox church with bright blue domes, was rebuilt in the 1990s after being used as a gymnasium in the Soviet years.

Even more unusual is the Dungan Mosque, built in 1910 by Chinese craftsmen for the Dungans, Chinese-speaking Muslims who fled to Central Asia in the nineteenth century. It looks like a Buddhist pagoda, with sweeping eaves, carved wood and bright paint, and it is said to have been built without a single nail. The Dungans also brought their food, and Karakol is one of the best places in Central Asia to eat it. Ashlan-fu, a cold, spicy noodle dish with jelly-like starch and vinegar, is a local speciality, served at stalls near the market.

Karakol is the starting point for the high mountains. A road leads up the Karakol Valley to an alpine base for trekking, and in winter the nearby ski resort draws visitors. The Russian explorer Nikolai Przhevalsky, who set out from here on expeditions across Central Asia, died in Karakol in 1888 and is buried nearby, and a museum commemorates him.

For riders, Karakol is a comfortable base. There are plenty of guesthouses, cafes and shops, petrol is easy to find, and mechanics can sort out problems. The roads around the lake are mostly paved, though sections can be broken, with potholes and loose gravel, and livestock often wander across. Wind can blow strongly along the shore in the afternoon.

In the evening, the old town takes on a gentle, rural atmosphere, with smoke from stoves, the call to prayer and the sound of a distant radio. It is an agreeable place to spend a night or two before heading into the mountains.
t.naryn@41.4,76.0:
Naryn lies in a long, narrow valley in the heart of the Tian Shan, at about two thousand metres, and the pin lands in the town centre, beside the river that gives the place its name. It is the capital of the province and the last real town of any size before the high pastures, a low, grey Soviet-era place of apartment blocks and a few older buildings, with brown hills rising on both sides and snowy peaks beyond. Winters are bitterly cold, sometimes thirty below, while summers are dry and bright.

The road from here leads to some of the most remote and spectacular country in Central Asia. Song-Köl, a vast alpine lake at around three thousand metres, sits in a high plateau where herders bring their sheep, horses and yaks every summer and live in yurts. The tracks that lead to it are rough, with gravel, steep gradients and fords, and the lake is usually accessible only from June to September, since snow blocks the passes for the rest of the year. Altitude and weather change fast, and a sunny morning can turn to hail by afternoon, so bring warm and waterproof clothing.

Naryn has an old connection with the Silk Road. About a hundred kilometres to the south-west, the stone caravanserai of Tash Rabat, a fortified rest stop thought to date from the fifteenth century, stands in a lonely valley, and the road beyond leads over the Torugart pass, at 3,752 metres, to China. Kyrgyz culture here is one of horses and storytelling, and the epic of Manas, a hero poem many times longer than the Iliad, is still recited by singers. Hospitality is generous, and a visitor in a yurt is offered tea, bread and kumys, fermented mare's milk, which is an acquired taste.

Fuel is available in Naryn, with several stations, and it is essential to fill up and carry extra, since the high country has none. Cafes along the main street serve beshbarmak, boiled meat with noodles, laghman noodle soup and manty dumplings, and the bazaar sells bread, fruit and dairy products.

Check your bike over before you leave. The tracks are long and help is far away, and a calm start makes the rest of the journey easier.
t.kolsai lakes@42.9,78.3:
Kolsai Lakes are three alpine lakes strung out in a valley of the Kungey Alatau range, in the far south-east of Kazakhstan, close to the Kyrgyz border. The first lies at around 1,800 metres, and the second, reached by a longer walk, at about 2,250, with a third higher still in the mountains. The water is a deep, cold turquoise, held between steep slopes of dark spruce, and the reflections of the forest and the sky in the still surface make a memorable sight. The lakes were formed by landslides that blocked the valley, long ago.

The forests of Tien Shan spruce around them are home to deer, lynx and, rarely, brown bears, and the lakes are stocked with trout. A national park protects the area. Visitors come to walk, ride horses and camp, and the valley is much quieter than it might be, with only a handful of guesthouses and yurt camps near the first lake. At night, the stars are brilliant, and the air is thin and cold. Even in summer, the temperature can drop close to freezing, so bring warm clothing.

The road to the lakes passes through the village of Saty, where families rent rooms and offer homemade food, and then climbs to a car park by the first lake. The surface is a mixture of tarmac and rough track, with loose stones, potholes and sometimes mud, and heavy rain can make it difficult. The best season is from June to September, when the snow has melted. In winter, the road is often blocked by snow.

Fuel stations are scarce in this region. Tyup, across the border in Kyrgyzstan, is the nearest town noted here, but crossing the border requires the proper papers, and on the Kazakh side the town of Kegen is the more usual choice. Fill your tank before you leave, carry a spare can if you can, and bring food and water.

The Charyn Canyon, a long day's ride to the north-west, is the other great sight of this route, and offers a contrast in colour and drama.
t.kaindy lake@43.0,78.5:
Kaindy is a lake with a ghostly forest. When an earthquake shook the Tian Shan in January 1911, a landslide dammed a valley, and the water that backed up flooded a stand of Schrenk's spruce. The trunks of the drowned trees still stand upright in the water, bare and pale, preserved by the cold, and the lake itself is a deep, clear turquoise. It lies at around two thousand metres, in the Kolsai Lakes National Park, in the mountains of south-eastern Kazakhstan, close to the border with Kyrgyzstan.

The way there is part of the adventure. The road from Saty, the last village, climbs on a rough track of gravel and stones, with steep gradients, ruts and stream crossings, and is best suited to a trail bike or 4x4. The last stretch is on foot or by a local shuttle, depending on the season and the state of the road. Conditions vary after rain, when the track can turn to mud. Roads are normally open from late spring to autumn, and snow blocks the area for the winter months. The water is cold even in summer, so swimming is not advised, and the sight of the sunken trees is best from the shore.

Nearby, the Kolsai Lakes, three alpine lakes at different heights, lie among spruce forests, and the Charyn Canyon, a long red sandstone gorge sometimes called the Valley of Castles, lies within a day's drive. The area is part of the old nomad lands of the Kazakhs, and herders still bring horses to the high pastures in summer. The nearest town on the Kyrgyz side is Tyup, about thirty kilometres away, but the border zone has rules, and foreign visitors should check permit requirements before they travel.

Fuel is not available at the lake, so fill up before the final approach, in Kegen or the larger centres, and carry extra if your tank is small. Guesthouses in Saty serve simple meals of soup, bread and local honey, and tea is always offered.

Go early in the day. The light on the water is clearest in the morning, and the quiet is complete.
t.moldo ashuu pass@41.8,75.3:
Moldo Ashuu is a high, bare pass on the track that leads into the Song Kol plateau from the south, at about 3,350 metres, and it is the sort of place that makes you feel small in a very good way. The road climbs out of the valley of the Naryn region in dusty switchbacks over rolling hills, crosses a ridge of scree and short grass, and tops out among prayer-flag-less cairns and the wind. There is no town and no hut. Marmots whistle from their burrows and the horizon is made of long, soft brown ridges. Ashuu is the Kyrgyz word for pass, and the Kyrgyz have a habit of naming each one after something about it, which keeps the map honest.

The road is gravel, sometimes graded and sometimes not, with stretches of washboard, loose stones, stream crossings and the occasional bit of mud. It is a proper adventure road, and it needs a bike that can handle it and a rider with some experience of dirt. Weather matters a great deal at this altitude. Snow can fall on the pass in any month, including midsummer, storms build quickly, and the road is closed completely by deep snow from about October to May. Even in summer, the temperature can drop to freezing at night and the wind is hard. Carry warm clothes, rain gear and food, and tell someone where you are going.

The reward is the highland beyond. Song Kol, a high-altitude lake, lies about three thousand metres above the sea and is used in summer as pasture by herders who bring their sheep, horses and cattle up from the valleys and live in felt yurts. These seasonal pastures, called jailoo, are a centre of Kyrgyz life and culture. Visitors can stay in yurt camps in July and August, drinking kymyz, fermented mare's milk, and eating bread, cream and mutton.

Naryn and Kochkor are the nearest towns with stations and supplies, so start with a full tank and a spare can if you have one. Phone signal is patchy or absent. Water from streams should be treated or boiled, and altitude sickness is a possibility for those who ascend too quickly, so take time to adjust.

The best time to come is July to early September. The days are warm, the flowers are out and the grass is green, but the nights are cold, so a warm sleeping bag is welcome.
t.song kol@41.9,75.2:
Song Kol is a lake on the roof of Kyrgyzstan, a broad sheet of cold blue water at about three thousand metres, surrounded by treeless grass hills and an enormous sky. It is the second largest lake in the country after Issyk-Kul, and in the short summer it is the heart of the nomadic world. Shepherd families move up from the valleys with their flocks, set up their yurts along the shore, and spend a few months on the high pastures, and the whole plateau is dotted with white tents, horses and sheep. In the evening, the herds come down to the water, the smoke rises from the yurt chimneys and the light turns the hills gold.

There are no villages and no roads in the strict sense, just gravel tracks that link the passes and the yurt camps. Getting here involves one of the high passes, from Kochkor in the north or the Naryn side in the south, and the tracks are rough, with washboard, sand patches and the odd stream to ford. The ride is demanding, particularly if it has rained, when clay surfaces become slippery. Distances are long and the altitude affects both bikes and riders. The lake is accessible only in summer, usually from June to September, and it is frozen for much of the rest of the year, with deep snow on the plateau.

The weather is the main hazard. Storms with hail and lightning can sweep across the open plain, and temperatures at night can fall below freezing even in July. Be prepared for all conditions and carry warm clothes, even if the afternoon feels pleasant. In the thin air, the stars at night are astonishing, with the Milky Way across the whole sky and no light pollution at all.

Staying in a yurt camp is part of the experience, and local families offer beds, meals and horse rides at modest prices, arranged by community organisations or simply by turning up. The food is simple, with bread, jam, cream, noodles and meat, and the drink of choice is kymyz, which is an acquired taste. Horse riding is a good way to explore the shore, and locals will happily lead you. Eagles and other raptors circle overhead, and in the marshes at the edge of the lake, waterfowl nest in summer.

Plan your tank and carry extra from Kochkor or Naryn, and bring spare tubes, tools and food. Phone signal is poor, so travel with others if you can.

The place is a window onto a way of life that is changing but still alive. Be respectful, ask before photographing people, and leave no trace.
t.kalmak ashuu pass@42.1,75.3:
Kalmak Ashuu is the northern gate to the Song Kol plateau, a pass of about 3,450 metres on the track that climbs out of the Kochkor valley, and it is the one that most riders take when coming from Bishkek or Issyk-Kul. The name means something like the pass of the Kalmyks, and tradition links it to the Oirat peoples who moved through this region centuries ago, though like many Central Asian place names the origin is half legend. The road leaves the valley floor and climbs in a series of long switchbacks across dry hills, past clusters of yurts and flocks of sheep, to a saddle of bare grass and rock with a great view to the south over the plateau.

The surface is gravel for most of the way, sometimes smooth and sometimes badly corrugated, with sections of loose stone and short rocky steps. It is the more popular of the routes to Song Kol, so it is generally better maintained and busier, though still a serious road after rain or snowmelt. Streams cross the track in places and the water can be deep in spring. The upper section has some steep, exposed bends where care is needed, and the weather at the top can turn quickly, with strong winds and sudden snow. In winter the road is closed and heavy snow lies on the pass until late spring.

From the top you look across to a wide upland of grass, with the lake glinting in the distance, and on a clear day the Tien Shan ranges stand around the horizon in layers of blue. The air is thin and cold, even in summer, and the silence is broken only by the wind and the whistle of marmots. It is a place for taking pictures and taking breath, in either order.

Fill the tank in Kochkor, which has stations and shops, and carry spare fuel for the plateau, since the round trip to the lake and back is long. A small shop or tea stall may appear in the villages on the way up, but do not count on it. Carry water, snacks and a warm layer, and a repair kit for the bike.

Altitude can cause headaches in people who arrive from low ground, so it is wise to spend a night or two at moderate height first. Start early, since afternoon storms are common and the descent is better done in good light.
t.petropolis@-22.5,-43.2:
For decades, the emperors of Brazil escaped the Rio summer by climbing into these hills, and Petrópolis still feels like an imperial retreat. The city lies in the Serra dos Órgãos at around 800 metres, cooler and fresher than the coast, and it was built in the mid-nineteenth century as a summer residence for Dom Pedro II, the last emperor. His former palace is now the Imperial Museum, where visitors shuffle across the polished floors in felt slippers to protect them, and it holds the crown jewels.

Walking around the centre you see a city planned by an engineer, with canals running through the streets, German-style houses, a neo-Gothic cathedral where the emperor and his family are buried, and the Crystal Palace, a greenhouse of iron and glass. The aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont also built a small house here, which he called A Encantada, and you can visit it. In the region there is an old beer-brewing tradition, and the town is known for chocolate shops and cafés.

For motorcyclists, the road up from Rio is a classic. The BR-040 climbs the escarpment of the Serra da Estrela in long ramps through dense forest, steep and busy with lorries, and in the mist it can feel eerie. Taking the road on toward Teresópolis you leave the main highways and follow quieter routes through the hills with tree-lined avenues, green valleys and the occasional waterfall. The weather changes quickly, with fog and rain common, so take waterproofs, and be careful on wet cobbles in the old streets.

This is a large city of about two hundred and seventy thousand people, so there is plenty of fuel, mechanics and restaurants, and Guapimirim and Teresópolis are the next centres. Weekends fill up with visitors from Rio, so a midweek visit is easier. Climate is mild and often damp, so a light rain jacket is as useful as a sweater. Stop for a hot chocolate in the afternoon, and set off for the next leg while the light is still good, since the mountain roads are no fun in the dark.
t.teresopolis@-22.4,-43.0:
Look up from the streets of Teresópolis and you will see the Dedo de Deus, the Finger of God, a granite spire that points at the sky from the ridge above town. It is the emblem of the Serra dos Órgãos, a range whose jagged peaks reminded the Portuguese of organ pipes, and the city sits right beside the national park that protects it. Altitude is around 900 metres, so evenings are cool, and in winter you may need a jacket.

The city grew in the nineteenth century as a mountain retreat for Rio's wealthy and the imperial family, and was named for the empress Teresa Cristina. Today it is a busy place of more than a hundred and twenty thousand people, with a mix of old villas, university buildings and shopping streets, and is also the training base of Brazil's national football team, which has a centre here. The Serra dos Órgãos National Park is one of the oldest in the country, with trails to viewpoints, waterfalls and the long climb to the summit of the Pedra do Sino, the highest point in the range.

On the bike, the road from Petrópolis through Itaipava is a favourite weekend run, with gentle climbs and drops between ridges, small valleys full of nurseries and flower farms, and bends that suit a relaxed pace. From Teresópolis, the road toward Rio drops off the escarpment in a spectacular descent through forest, with tight bends, heavy lorries and fog that sometimes covers the upper part, so be cautious. Sunday evening traffic going back toward the coast is slow.

Fuel and services are plentiful, since São Pedro is practically joined to the city, and Guapimirim, a short ride downhill, is another town to rely on. The city is known for its restaurants, with trout dishes and mountain-style food, and the fruit and vegetable markets sell produce from the hills. Early morning is the best time for a ride or walk, when the peaks are clear before clouds build in the afternoon. Bring a light waterproof, as showers arrive suddenly, and keep an eye on the weather forecast if you plan to go into the park.
t.ilha grande state park@-23.2,-44.2:
Off the coast of Rio de Janeiro state, between Rio and Paraty, Ilha Grande rises from the sea, a mountainous island covered in Atlantic rainforest, with dozens of beaches, coves and waterfalls. For much of the twentieth century, it was home to a notorious prison and a leper colony, which kept development at bay, and today, most of the island is protected as a state park. It is part of the UNESCO site Paraty and Ilha Grande, Culture and Biodiversity, listed in 2019.

There are no cars on the island, apart from a few official vehicles, so getting around is by foot or by boat. The main village, Abraão, is a lively place with guesthouses, restaurants and bars, and from there, trails lead through the forest to beaches such as Lopes Mendes, often ranked among the most beautiful in Brazil, and to the ruins of the old prison at Dois Rios. The forest is home to monkeys, toucans and other wildlife, and the waters around the island are clear and warm, perfect for snorkelling and diving.

The ride to the coast is a highlight in its own right. The Rio–Santos highway, the BR-101, runs along the Costa Verde, between the mountains of the Serra do Mar and the sea, with curves, climbs and views of islands, bays and beaches. Traffic can be heavy, especially on weekends and holidays, and the road can be slippery in rain. Boats to Ilha Grande leave from Angra dos Reis, Conceição de Jacareí and Mangaratiba, so you will need to park your bike on the mainland, ideally in a secure car park.

Angra dos Reis and Mangaratiba have fuel, shops and restaurants. The local cuisine is based on seafood, such as moqueca, a fish stew with coconut milk and palm oil, and fried fish with rice and beans. Bring sun protection, insect repellent and good shoes for the trails, and take your time to enjoy the island's relaxed pace.
t.sitio roberto burle marx@-23.0,-43.5:
Roberto Burle Marx changed the way the world thought about gardens. The Brazilian landscape architect, painter and plant collector, who died in 1994, designed the wave-patterned promenade along Copacabana beach, the gardens of the Ministry of Education in Rio, and hundreds of other parks and gardens, using native tropical plants in bold, abstract compositions. In 1949 he bought a former coffee estate in Barra de Guaratiba, in the far west of Rio de Janeiro, and turned it into his home, studio and laboratory, filling it with thousands of plant species collected on expeditions across Brazil. Sítio Roberto Burle Marx was added to the World Heritage list in 2021.

The estate is a place of extraordinary beauty, with lush gardens, pools, rock walls covered in bromeliads, a small colonial chapel, and the house where Burle Marx lived and worked, full of his paintings and collections of folk art. Visits are by guided tour, and they are well worth booking in advance. The setting, between forested hills and the mangroves of the Guaratiba lagoon, adds to the magic.

Riding to the Sítio is a chance to explore a different side of Rio. The western zone of the city is less crowded than the famous beaches of the south, with a coastline of wild beaches backed by forested hills. The road from Recreio dos Bandeirantes to Barra de Guaratiba passes the beaches of Prainha and Grumari, part of a protected area, with steep, winding sections over the headlands, and views over the ocean that are as good as anything in the city. The road can be busy at weekends, when locals head for the beaches, and surfaces are sometimes rough.

Rio traffic, in general, is heavy and aggressive, and motorcycle riders need to be alert, especially on the expressways and in the tunnels. Fuel is easy to find, but it is wise to ride in daylight, keep valuables out of sight and seek local advice about safe routes. Barra de Guaratiba is a small fishing village with seafood restaurants, especially good for fresh fish and shrimp. The climate is hot and humid, with heavy rain in summer, from December to March, and milder, drier weather in winter, the best time for riding.
t.environmental protection area of cairucu:
Between the old colonial port of Paraty and the border of São Paulo state, the mountains of the Serra do Mar come down to the sea in a jumble of forested peaks, rocky headlands and small, perfect bays, and the Cairuçu Environmental Protection Area covers much of this coast. It is part of the World Heritage site of Paraty and Ilha Grande, inscribed in 2019 for its combination of cultural and natural values. The forest here is the Mata Atlântica, the Atlantic rainforest, one of the richest and most threatened ecosystems on the planet, home to monkeys, toucans, hummingbirds and countless species of orchids and bromeliads. Within the area lie fishing villages of caiçaras, the traditional coastal people, and settlements of quilombolas, descendants of escaped slaves, as well as Guarani villages.

Paraty itself was built in the eighteenth century as the port through which gold from Minas Gerais was shipped to Portugal, and its old centre has hardly changed, with white houses, colourful doors and windows, and streets paved with large irregular stones. The streets are designed to flood at high tide, letting the sea wash them clean. The area around has long been known for its cachaça, the sugarcane spirit, and there are many small distilleries to visit.

The Rio-Santos highway, BR-101, runs along the coast through Paraty, one of the most beautiful roads in Brazil, winding between the mountains and the sea with views over the bays and islands. It is busy at weekends and holidays, and the surface can be broken in places, with landslides after heavy rain. The road to Trindade, a village of beaches and natural pools south of Paraty, is steep and twisty, and the road from Paraty up to Cunha, over the mountains, climbs very steeply through the forest, an old gold trail of the Estrada Real, now paved. Rain is frequent all year, and the roads become slippery.

Paraty has fuel, hotels, restaurants and shops, and it is the natural base for exploring the area. The historic centre is closed to vehicles, so park outside and walk, carefully, on the uneven stones. Try fresh fish, shrimp in coconut sauce and a caipirinha made with local cachaça. Take a boat trip to the bays and islands, where the water is warm and clear, a fitting end to a day's riding.
t.paraty and ilha grande culture and biodi:
There are few places where a rainforest drops directly into the sea, and the coast between Rio and Santos is one of them. Paraty sits at the edge of a bay, with the mountains of the Serra da Bocaina rising steeply behind and the green islands of the bay scattered in front. The town was founded in the seventeenth century and prospered as the port where gold from the mines of Minas Gerais was shipped to Rio and on to Portugal, brought down the mountain on the Gold Road, the Caminho do Ouro, which you can still walk in places. UNESCO listed Paraty and Ilha Grande in 2019, as a landscape of culture and biodiversity.

The centre of Paraty is a pleasant surprise, with whitewashed colonial houses, painted doors and streets paved with large uneven stones, closed to cars, which are laid so that the tide floods them a few times a month, washing the streets clean. In the bay, the island of Ilha Grande has long beaches and forest with no cars, and it once held a notorious prison that closed in the 1990s. The surrounding Atlantic Forest is among the most biodiverse on Earth, with monkeys, toucans and orchids.

For riding, the Rio–Santos highway, the BR-101, is a classic, with a long run of bends along the coast, views over bays and islands, and a lot of trucks and holiday traffic. It is better on weekdays and in the morning, and rain and fog can arrive quickly. Another good route climbs inland from Paraty up the old road to Cunha, with hairpins through forest, to a cooler plateau known for its ceramics. Surfaces are variable, and potholes and landslides can appear after heavy rain, which falls mostly from December to March.

Paraty has fuel, cafes and plenty of restaurants, and the town is known for its cachaça, the sugar-cane spirit, which is made in small distilleries nearby. Fresh seafood, such as fish stew cooked in coconut milk, is excellent. Parking in the old town is limited, so leave the bike in a hotel or paid lot, and take care at night, when the streets are quiet. Ferries to Ilha Grande leave from the nearby town of Angra dos Reis, and from Conceição de Jacareí, and you need to book.
t.pedra bonita and pedra da gavea tijuca n:
Two granite monoliths stand over the western edge of Rio de Janeiro, and they draw very different crowds. Pedra da Gávea, at about eight hundred and forty metres, is a massive block with a flat face that looks, from some angles, like a human profile, and it has attracted legends, including one about Phoenician inscriptions carved by sailors thousands of years ago. Experts think the marks are natural erosion. Pedra Bonita, a smaller sister, is where hang-gliders and paragliders launch from a wooden ramp, floating down over the forest to land on the beach at São Conrado, in one of the most photographed flights in the world.

Both are part of Tijuca National Park, a patch of Atlantic rainforest that stands inside a city of six million people, and which UNESCO included in its listing of the Carioca landscapes in 2012. Remarkably, the forest is largely man-made. In the nineteenth century, deforestation for coffee and charcoal threatened the city's water supply, and Emperor Pedro II ordered the hillside to be replanted, a project begun in 1861 under Major Archer, who planted tens of thousands of saplings. Today it supports monkeys, toucans and sloths.

The riding around Rio is exhilarating and tricky. The Estrada das Canoas winds up through the forest to the Tijuca massif with views over the lagoon and the sea, and the corniche roads along the coast are a pleasure, though traffic is heavy and drivers are fast. Rain can arrive suddenly and make the cobbles and painted lines slippery, and potholes, buses and motorbike couriers all require attention. As in any big city, take security seriously, avoid unfamiliar neighbourhoods, especially at night, and keep valuables out of sight.

Fuel and food are available everywhere in the city, with plenty of stations on the main roads and small snack bars selling fresh coconut water and pastries. The hike to the top of Pedra da Gávea is long and steep, with an exposed scramble at the end, and requires a guide, while Pedra Bonita is an easier walk. Start early, because the clouds often come in by midday, and take water.
t.morro da vila velha@-23.2,-44.7:
Paraty sits between the mountains and the sea, and Morro da Vila Velha, a hill beside the old town, is a good vantage for seeing why. The mountains of the Serra do Mar rise steeply behind, covered in Atlantic forest, and the bay in front is dotted with islands. Portuguese settlers took the site in the sixteenth century, and in the eighteenth it became the port for gold from Minas Gerais, carried down the Caminho do Ouro on mule trains and loaded onto ships. UNESCO listed Paraty and Ilha Grande together in 2019, recognising both the culture and the nature.

The historic centre is a delight, with whitewashed colonial houses, painted doors and streets paved with rounded stones, laid so that the high tides can flood and flush them. Cars are barred from the core, and the stones are punishing on a loaded bike, so park and walk. The town is small, with about fifteen thousand people, and it has fuel, restaurants, bars and plenty of guesthouses. Paraty is famous for cachaça, the cane spirit, and for the literary festival held every year.

The ride to get here is one of Brazil's finest. The BR-101, the Rio-Santos road, hugs the coast between the sea and the forest, with long curves, island views and beaches tucked into every bay. Traffic is heavy at weekends and holidays, so go midweek if you can. Inland, the road to Cunha climbs the Serra do Mar in a series of hairpins through mist-soaked forest, a great contrast, though rain makes it slippery and landslides are possible.

Humidity is high, and downpours are common between December and March, when the roads can flood. June to August is drier and cooler, with clear days and fewer crowds. Ilha Grande, a short boat trip away, has no cars at all, and the Praia do Sul biological reserve is protected, with strict access rules. Order fresh fish, moqueca, or a banana-based dessert, and linger at a table on the square as the lamps come on.
t.altyn emel central@43.9,78.7:
The central part of Altyn-Emel, in south-eastern Kazakhstan, is a landscape of space more than anything else. The national park lies between the Ili River and the Dzungarian Alatau, a couple of hundred kilometres east of Almaty, and its name is often translated as golden saddle. The land is steppe and semi-desert in broad swathes of dusty yellow, broken here and there by dry gullies, clumps of saxaul and the strange coloured hills of the Aktau mountains, where layers of white, pink and orange clay look as though they were painted on. This is the geology of an old sea bed, tilted and eroded.

There is wildlife here that you can actually see if you are patient. The kulan, or wild ass, is common on the plains. Goitered gazelle bound away from the vehicle, and the Przewalski's horse was brought back into the park in the early 2000s as part of a reintroduction effort. Saker falcons and eagles circle overhead, and the Singing Dune, a long sandy ridge that hums in dry weather when the sand slides, is one of the park's best-known sights. The Saka people, who were nomadic horse riders, left burial mounds across the area that go back more than two thousand years.

Being honest, this is not asphalt riding country. The roads inside the park are tracks, sandy in places and rough in others, and much of the best of it is in a protected area where you will need permission to enter, and in some cases a guide. The border with China is close, and special rules apply, so check what is needed before you set out. Summer is hot, with temperatures often passing forty degrees, and winters are bitterly cold and windy. Spring, when the steppe is briefly green and flowering, and early autumn are the best seasons.

The area sits at the edge of the Cold Winter Deserts of Turan, and the sense of emptiness is the very point of coming here.
t.paraty historic center@-23.2,-44.7:

t.paraty@-23.2,-44.7:

t.praia do sul biological reserve@-23.2,-4:

t.city of nevaket@42.9,75.0:

t.altyn emel west@44.0,78.3:
Altyn-Emel means golden saddle, and when the evening sun hits the ridge it is easy to see why. Raptors circle above the ridges, and in the Ili valley, dense riverside forest grows against the desert. Permits and a small fee are required at the park entrance, and the rangers can help with directions. t.rio de janeiro@-22.9,-43.2:

t.angra dos reis@-23.0,-44.3:

t.mouth of guanabara bay and manmade shore:

t.balykchy@42.5,76.2:
Balykchy is at the far western end of Issyk-Kul, the second-largest mountain lake in the world, and its name in Kyrgyz means fisherman. t.charyn canyon@43.4,79.1:

The gorge runs for about a hundred and fifty kilometres, reaching depths of around three hundred metres, and the most visited stretch is the Valley of Castles, where wind and water have carved the red sandstone into towers, arches and ramparts that seem to have been built by giants. In the early morning or the evening, the light is soft and the air is cooler, and the ride is more comfortable than at midday.

t.trindade@-23.3,-44.6:

t.itanhandu@-22.3,-44.9:

t.cold winter deserts of turan@44.0,79.0:
Turan is the name of the great lowland that stretches across Central Asia, from the Caspian to the foothills of the Tian Shan, and its cold winter deserts are one of the continent's lesser-known biomes. The coordinates sit in the Altyn-Emel National Park in south-eastern Kazakhstan, along the Ili river, in a landscape of sand, clay and sparse grass where summers burn and winters freeze, and the sky is huge.

The park's most famous feature is the Singing Dune, a sand ridge about a hundred and fifty metres high and three kilometres long that hums or booms when the sand slides, with a sound some compare to a low organ or an aircraft engine. Around it the desert holds saxaul, a tough, twisted tree that survives on almost no water, and tracks of foxes, hares and lizards in the dust.

Wildlife is the other attraction. Kulan, the Asian wild ass, roam in herds and have been reintroduced, along with Przewalski's horses released in recent years, and goitered gazelles move across the plains. Golden eagles and steppe eagles ride the thermals above. The park has a sparse network of tracks, and a ranger-guided jeep tour is the usual way to visit, since access is regulated and navigation is tricky. Heat in July can pass forty degrees, and spring brings flowers and storms.

For a rider, the key is preparation. The main road to the park gate from Almaty is a long drive over the Kapchagay reservoir area, and beyond the gate surfaces are sand and gravel, unsuitable for most road motorcycles. Fill up in Almaty or the last big town before the park, carry water and food, and expect to pay an entry fee and often to join a guided vehicle. The reward is silence, wide skies and a night of stars.
t.altyn emel east@44.0,79.0:
Altyn-Emel means golden saddle, and legend says it takes the name from the shape of a pass between two ranges. The park lies between the Dzungarian Alatau to the north and the Ili river and Kapchagay reservoir to the south, and its east side is a country of coloured hills. The Aktau mountains show cliffs of white, yellow and pink clay and sandstone, banded like layer cake, and the Katutau hills nearby offer ochre and rust. At sunset the colours seem lit from within.

People have been here for millennia. The park holds many burial mounds, kurgans, of the Saka, the nomadic horsemen the Greeks called Scythians, and the Besshatyr group, with its large mounds in a line like a row of loaves, is the most impressive. The Silk Road passed through the Ili valley, and caravans moved between China and the west along it, so the region is full of traces of trade and passage. Rock carvings, petroglyphs of ibex and hunters, are found in the canyons.

Fuel should be filled in Almaty or at towns along the main road, such as Kapchagay, and water, food, and a spare tyre kit are important. The park charges entry and has rules about camping. A guide from the park will take you to the best viewpoints. Allow a full day and stay for sunset.
t.kochkor@42.2,75.8:
Kochkor is a flat, windy, high-valley town at roughly eighteen hundred metres in Kyrgyzstan's Naryn region, and it is where riders turn from the pavement to the dirt. It sits in a broad valley between the Kyrgyz Ala-Too and the Kyoktu range, with sheep and horses in the fields around it and the long line of the mountains marked by snow in all but the hottest months. About two hundred kilometres from Bishkek, it is the usual gateway to Song-Kol, a high alpine lake at over three thousand metres where herders bring their flocks in summer.

Women's cooperatives here make shyrdak and ala-kiyiz, the colourful felt carpets that cover the floors of yurts, using techniques that go back centuries, and a visit to a workshop is a good way to understand how closely the culture is tied to the animals. The wool is washed, dyed, rolled and pressed by hand, and the designs, spirals, horns and tree-like patterns, have meanings. A community tourism office in the town arranges homestays and rides.

The road from Bishkek is the pleasure of the journey. It follows the Chu River through the Boom Gorge, a narrow canyon with red rock walls, and then crosses the plateau past the western end of Lake Issyk-Kul, a huge blue lake ringed by snowy mountains. The pavement is generally decent, though trucks and rough patches are common, and cattle and horses wander across without warning. Weather can change quickly, and in spring and autumn snow can fall even on the lower passes. The Song-Kol road, beyond Kochkor, is gravel, steep and closed by snow outside the summer months, so check conditions with local guides before you go.

Kochkor has fuel and basic shops, and it is the last reliable place to fill before the mountains. Carry spare fuel for the high tracks, along with warm layers and food. Try the traditional bread, baked in a clay oven, and a bowl of fermented mare's milk if you are curious. Summer is the best season, with long evenings and wildflowers on the high pastures.
t.city of suyab@42.8,75.2:
Suyab was a Silk Road city, and it lies in a field. About nine kilometres from the town of Tokmok, in the wide Chu Valley of northern Kyrgyzstan, the low mounds of Ak-Beshim mark the remains of a Sogdian trading town that was later a capital of the Western Turkic Khaganate and a Tang-dynasty frontier outpost. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang passed through in 629 and described a bustling place with merchants from many lands, and a local tradition even holds that the poet Li Bai was born here, though historians argue about it.

The site is quiet now. You can see the outline of walls, the foundations of a Buddhist temple and a Nestorian Christian church, which tells you how mixed the town's population was, and archaeologists have found Chinese coins, Sogdian inscriptions and Buddhist statues.
