The main road east along the Chu Valley is paved and often busy, running along a plain of farmland, with the high Kyrgyz Ala-Too range standing white along the southern horizon. Trucks, minibuses and the occasional horse cart share the road, and the road surface is variable, with patches of damage. The approach to the sites is by smaller roads through villages and fields, where dogs and livestock are the main hazards.

Tokmok has about sixty-three thousand people and is the sensible place to buy fuel, water and snacks, since there is nothing at the ruins themselves. Summer is hot and dusty, spring and autumn are milder, and winter brings cold winds. The wind on the open plain can be strong, so a light jacket is useful. Allow time to walk across the mounds, imagine the camel caravans, and take a few photographs of the mountains behind.
t.song kol@41.8,75.1:
Song Kol is a lake at 3,000 metres, sitting in a high bowl of the Tian Shan like something left behind by the sky. Its name means last lake, or perhaps following lake; Kyrgyz speakers give different readings. It lies in Naryn province, far from any town, and for four months a year it is the summer pasture of herders who bring their sheep, horses and yaks up from the valleys. Their yurts, white domes against a green and brown landscape, are the main architecture here, and the main way a traveller stays.

Reaching the lake is a proper expedition on two wheels. The usual approach climbs from the Kochkor valley over a pass at roughly 3,400 metres on gravel roads with a series of tight hairpins, steep drops and variable surface. Loose stones, mud after rain, and stream crossings are all possible, and a bike with decent ground clearance and tyres is a real advantage. The track along the shore is open and rolling, with big skies, no trees, a constant wind, and horses moving across the pasture. It is wonderful riding, but not casual riding.

The season is short. The road is generally passable from about June to September, with the weather closing in sooner than you might expect. Even in July, nights are cold enough for frost, and the wind can cut straight through a summer jacket. Dress like it is autumn, whatever the calendar says. In the right conditions, though, the lake mirrors the clouds and the mountains, and the sound of hooves and sheep bells carries for miles. At night the stars arrive in ridiculous numbers.

Fill up at Kochkor or Naryn before you head in, carry spare fuel if your range is limited, and bring a tool kit. Yurt camps offer a bed, dinner and breakfast, typically bread, jam, soup, mutton and plenty of tea, plus sometimes kymyz, fermented mare's milk. Be respectful of the herders' land and animals, take your rubbish with you, and ride out with the feeling that you have been somewhere that genuinely feels far away.
t.tash rabat@40.8,75.3:
Tash Rabat is a stone building in the middle of nowhere, which is exactly why it still stands. A caravanserai, one of the inns that sheltered Silk Road traders, it sits in a high, narrow valley south of Naryn at around 3,200 metres, tucked against a hillside and built from dark local stone with domed rooms around a central hall. The main structure is usually dated to the fifteenth century, though some researchers think the site is older and may have begun as a monastery, possibly Nestorian Christian, centuries earlier. Nobody knows for sure, which suits the atmosphere.

The valley feels like the edge of the world. Beyond it, the road continues toward the Torugart Pass and the Chinese border, one of the old arteries of trade between Kashgar and the Fergana valley. Caravans crossed from the east, camels and horses carrying silk, spices, tea and news, and a stop here offered safety, water and a roof. Inside, thick walls and small rooms keep out the wind, and the dim light and cool air carry the feeling of centuries of tired travellers.

The ride from Naryn passes through the Naryn river valley and the village of At-Bashi, then climbs onto a broad, treeless plateau. The road is mostly paved but with occasional rough patches, and it feels long and open, with few cars and many livestock. The valley narrows as you approach, with red cliffs, snow on the high peaks and the wind off the Tian Shan. Weather changes quickly, so expect sun, cold rain and perhaps a flurry of snow in a single afternoon, even in summer.

Fuel is limited to Naryn, around a hundred kilometres to the northwest, so arrive full, and in the same spirit bring water and snacks. Near the caravanserai you will find a few yurt camps and basic guesthouses, and a small fee is usually charged to enter the building. The summer months are best; outside them, snow and cold make the valley harsh. Give yourself time to sit on the grass, drink tea with the camp family and look at the hills. It is a place that rewards slowing down.
t.cholpon ata@42.6,77.1:
Cholpon-Ata is the unofficial capital of the Issyk-Kul north shore, a long string of beaches, guesthouses and Soviet-era holiday camps on the edge of a lake so big and deep that it feels like a sea. Issyk-Kul, which means warm lake, almost never freezes despite lying at about 1,600 metres, thanks to its depth and slight salinity. On the far side, the snowy ridges of the Terskey Ala-Too rise above the water, and on a clear day the contrast between blue lake, golden shore and white mountains is startling.

The town has about eighteen thousand people and a rhythm that changes dramatically with the seasons. In July and August, holidaymakers from Kazakhstan, Russia and Bishkek fill the beaches, and the main street is lined with cafes, souvenir stalls and fairground rides. In spring and autumn it is quiet and mild, and the lake is yours. Just outside town lies an open-air field of petroglyphs, boulders scattered across a grassy slope, carved with ibex, deer and hunters by people living here thousands of years ago, in what feels like a gallery laid out on a hillside.

The riding along the north shore is easy and pleasant. The road is mostly good tarmac with moderate traffic, passing through villages, orchards and small beaches, with the water on one side and the mountains on the other. It is not technical, but it is scenic, and you can set a relaxed pace and stop whenever you like. Watch out for cows, slow limits in the villages, and holiday traffic on summer weekends. The wind off the lake picks up in the afternoon, so mornings are calmer.

As a place to rest, Cholpon-Ata has everything: plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets, ATMs, hotels and guesthouses, and a whole street of restaurants serving fried lake fish, shashlik and fresh bread. Swimming is possible in summer, though the water is cool and slightly salty. It is a good place to take a day off, wash the dust from your gear and plan the next stretch, whether you are heading east toward Karakol or west back to the capital.
t.big almaty lake@43.1,77.0:
Big Almaty Lake is a turquoise bowl in the Trans-Ili Alatau, about 2,500 metres above sea level and a short way from a city of two million people. That contrast is the appeal. Almaty is a modern, busy city of malls and avenues, and yet within an hour you can be standing beside cold, glacier-fed water, with spruce forest on the lower slopes and bare, snow-streaked summits all around. The lake is a reservoir, and it supplies a good part of the city's drinking water, which explains why access is controlled.

That is where the gate comes in. The road climbs from the suburbs of Almaty through the Big Almaty gorge in a long series of bends, shaded by Tian Shan spruce and mountain apple and wild apricot trees, which is fitting, since Almaty's name is often linked to the word for apple and wild apple forests grow in these ranges. Rules on private vehicles in the protected zone have changed over the years, with restrictions, fees and shuttle options at various times, so check the current arrangement before you ride up. A gate or checkpoint is a normal part of the experience.

The riding on the way is steep and tight, with hairpins, short straights, sometimes heavy weekend traffic and a surface that can be patchy after winter. Rain and fog roll in quickly, and the temperature is much cooler than in the city, so bring layers. Early on a weekday morning is a good time, when the light is soft, the water often still, and the tour buses have not arrived. Autumn brings gold in the valley and fresh snow on the peaks, which makes the colour of the lake almost unreal.

Nearby, a Soviet-era observatory and the radio and cosmic-ray facilities on the ridge hint at the area's scientific history. Wild camping is not allowed in the protected area either. The lake is best treated as a glittering half-day trip, not an overnight, and respected as the city's water supply.
t.kolsai lakes@43.0,78.3:
The Kolsai Lakes are a chain of three alpine lakes strung up a valley in the Kungey Alatau, a range on the border with Kyrgyzstan. The lowest lake sits at roughly 1,800 metres, the middle at about 2,250 and the top at around 2,700, and each is smaller and colder than the last. They are often called the Pearls of the Tian Shan, which is the sort of name that sounds like marketing until you see the water, a cold, deep blue-green framed in dark spruce forest and sharp ridgelines.

A few kilometres away lies Kaindy, a lake with a weird and wonderful feature: the trunks of drowned spruce trees stand upright in the water, a ghostly forest preserved by the cold. It formed in a major earthquake in the early twentieth century, when a landslide dammed the valley and flooded the trees. The road to Kaindy is rough in places, and many visitors go by jeep, but riders on suitable bikes can reach it, with care, in dry conditions.

The ride up to Kolsai passes through the village of Saty, one of the last settlements before the mountains, and from there the road rises through green meadows and spruce woods. Surface varies from decent tarmac to gravel, with potholes and stream crossings, and horses and cattle wander freely. This is border country, so foreigners may need a permit for the national park and the border zone, and it makes sense to organise that in advance, through a guesthouse or in Almaty, rather than at a checkpoint. Summer is the main season; snow lingers on the upper trails into June.

Saty has homestays and small guesthouses that cook simple, hearty meals, with fresh bread, local honey, mutton soup and tea. Nights are cold even in summer, and mornings are the best time for the lakes, when the water is still and the light slants through the spruce. If you have time, walking the trail to the second lake is worth doing, a few hours of quiet forest and sound of water.
t.tamgaly@43.8,75.5:
Tamgaly is a canyon full of drawings made three thousand years ago. In the dry Anyrakay hills, northwest of Almaty and not far from the Ili river plain, thousands of petroglyphs are scratched into dark rock, many of them from the Bronze Age, with later layers added over the centuries. The site is on the UNESCO World Heritage list, and the carvings include figures with rayed, sun-like heads, dancers, animals, riders and scenes that seem to show ritual. The name is often explained as meaning a painted or marked place.

It is stark country. The ride out from Almaty crosses a wide plain, passes the Kapchagay reservoir area, and then goes on into semi-desert and low hills. The roads are fast and often straight, with a few long climbs, and the surface can be patchy, so keep an eye out for livestock and the occasional hole. The terrain is open steppe, tawny grass in spring, scorched and silver in high summer, and the sky is huge. Wind and heat are the main hazards; there is almost no shade, so take plenty of water and a hat.

At the site itself, the main carvings lie along a gorge, with a few of the most striking images on a small plateau or amphitheatre of rock, and walking between them takes an hour or two. Nomads probably gathered here to perform ceremonies, and some of the images show burial and sacrifice. Bronze Age herders, and later peoples, used these hills for grazing and ritual, and nearby are old stone burial mounds. A small visitor facility and a ranger can help with directions, but this is not an overbuilt attraction.

The sensible places to fill are in Almaty or the larger towns on the road, like Kapchagay. Take drinking water, snacks and sun protection, and aim for morning or late afternoon when the light is better for the carvings and the temperature is lower. Spring is the loveliest season, when the hills are green and the poppies and tulips come out; the best photography light comes low and gold on the rock.
t.medeu@43.2,77.1:
Medeu is a big, white, somewhat surreal sports arena in a mountain valley. At about 1,700 metres above sea level, in the Zailiysky Alatau gorge just above Almaty, it holds one of the highest outdoor speed-skating rinks in the world, opened in the Soviet era in the early 1950s. Thin air and hard, fast ice made the rink famous, and many world records were set here over the decades. A long staircase climbs beside the arena, a good test for riders who have been sitting down all day.

Just below it, you can see a large earthen dam. That structure, built in the 1960s, was constructed to protect Almaty from mudflows, called sel in Russian, which have repeatedly threatened the city. A huge flow in the early twentieth century had done terrible damage, and engineers blasted and shaped the mountainside to create the dam. It is a strong reminder that the beautiful hills above the city are active, wet and occasionally dangerous.

The road up from Almaty climbs through the valley of the Malaya Almatinka river, with trees, apartment blocks and then forest on both sides. The surface is generally good, the bends are broad, and you will share it with buses, taxis and Sunday drivers. On weekends and holidays it becomes a slow, crowded procession, so a weekday morning or evening suits a motorcycle far better. In cold weather, ice can linger on shaded corners long after the city has thawed. Parking for bikes is usually easy at the lower lots, but check the signs.

Medeu is the gateway to the high country: the road continues up to Shymbulak, and cable cars and trails lead higher still. The air is fresh and smells of spruce and cold water. There are cafes and small stands for tea, snacks and shashlik, but fuel is a matter for Almaty, about fifteen kilometres below, so start with a full tank. The place is lovely in autumn, when the hills are red and gold, and in winter, when skaters circle under snowy peaks. In summer, bring a jacket anyway, because shade comes with a chill.
t.shymbulak@43.1,77.1:
Shymbulak is the ski resort Almaty keeps above itself like a spare room. The base sits at around 2,200 metres in the Zailiysky Alatau, reached by a steep road above Medeu or by a gondola lift, and from there chairlifts and cable cars carry skiers higher, to slopes at over three thousand metres. In winter it fills with skiers and snowboarders from across Kazakhstan; in summer it is quieter, with hikers, mountain bikers and people simply escaping the heat of the city.

The ride up from Medeu is a short, steep workout. The road climbs in a series of tight bends and hairpins through spruce forest, with a sudden change in air temperature and light as you gain height. The surface is usually decent, but weather and winter can leave frost heave, rockfall debris and loose gravel on the edges. Traffic is the real difficulty, especially on weekends, when cars queue for parking at the top. A weekday morning is a better bet, and so is a late start in winter, once the sun has softened the ice.

The mountain scenery is first class. Behind the resort, the valley narrows into a wall of rock and snow, with the peaks of the Trans-Ili range showing sharp and white. Spruce forest covers the lower slopes, and in summer, alpine meadows are full of flowers. Weather can change quickly: sun, cloud and cold rain can follow one another within an hour, and in shoulder seasons snow can appear unexpectedly. It is always cooler than in Almaty, often by ten degrees or more, so a layer is wise.

At the base, a village of hotels, restaurants and cafes offers hot meals and drinks, and it makes a comfortable stop for lunch with a view. In winter, check whether the road requires chains or is closed during snowfall. It is not a place for racing, but a good one for sitting with a hot tea and looking up.
t.altyn emel@44.2,78.8:
Altyn Emel is a national park of enormous scale in the Ili river basin, east of Almaty, and its name is often translated as golden saddle. The land is flat steppe and desert plain, rimmed by two ranges of hills: the Aktau, white mountains, and the Katutau, a banded landscape of reds, oranges, yellows and greens, laid down in layers and baked by the sun. At sunset these hills glow, and photographers arrive from across the country to catch them.

The park's most famous feature is the Singing Dune, a huge sand ridge, around a hundred and fifty metres high and several kilometres long, that hums or booms under the right conditions, particularly in dry, hot weather when sand slides down its face. Nobody quite agrees on the exact mechanism, though the vibrations of sliding grains seem to be the cause. The sound is something between a distant aircraft and a cello, and it is an eerie experience when you hear it.

The park also protects wildlife that has returned thanks to reintroduction. Przewalski's horses, the only truly wild horses left, were brought back here, as were kulan, the Asiatic wild ass, and goitered gazelles roam the plains. Further into the park are ancient burial mounds of the Saka people, the Iron Age nomads often grouped with the Scythians, including the large Besshatyr mounds, where rich gold finds were made. This is a place where natural and human history overlap.

Entry requires a permit and a fee, and the tracks inside are mostly gravel and sand, so check conditions and consider going with a local guide or ranger. The weather swings from hot and dry in summer to cold and windy in winter, and in spring the plain is bright with grass. Camping and basic accommodation can be arranged near the entrance, and the star-filled night sky is a quiet bonus.
